newsitem.title: FRANCE: SOCCER-FRANCE WORRIED ABOUT EXODUS AS LEAGUE RESUMES.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-FRANCE WORRIED ABOUT EXODUS AS LEAGUE RESUMES.

text.p: The new French soccer season kicks off this Friday with France's top teams worried about the ever-increasing exodus of their star players.
Champions Monaco have suffered more than most from the malaise threatening the quality of the game in France as talent leaves French shores.

The team from the principality lost their best foreign players in the close season, headed by Brazil's Sonny Anderson who was sold to Barcelona for a club record fee, somewhere between $16.5 million and $20 million.

Belgian Enzo Scifo, Swiss Marco Grassi and Denmark's Dan Petersen also left Monaco -- and the French league -- while the club's only notable recruit so far is Chad's Japhet N'Doram, signed from Nantes.

And it is not just foreign stars that Monaco have let go. Some of their most gifted nationals are heading out of the country too. Patrick Blondeau signed for Sheffield Wednesday while Emmanuel Petit and Gilles Grimandi both joined former Monaco coach Arsene Wenger at Arsenal.
The transfer fees saw Monaco hit the cash jackpot but coach Jean Tigana was against the exodus of talent and has hinted he may not stay in the principality much longer.
A similar weariness at losing his best players each season prompted Nantes coach Jean-Claude Suaudeau to resign.
Third last season, Nantes lost the last two star players from their 1995 winning campaign, Claude Makelele -- to Marseille -- and N'Doram.

A clear indication that France has failed to follow England's lead and become a haven for soccer greats was that the most notable imports of the season were two experienced and talented players, but no stars.
Italy's Marco Simone joined Paris St Germain from AC Milan and French international Laurent Blanc left Barcelona to join Marseille.
With the help of Simone and gifted Frenchmen Florian Maurice and Franck Gava, who both headed for the capital from Lyon, Paris St Germain will once again start the season as clear favourites.
The Parisians are desperate for a title after agonisingly finishing second for the past three seasons, behind Nantes in 1995, Auxerre in 1996 and Monaco last season.
Marseille had a lacklustre return to the top flight last year after two seasons marred by financial and legal problems.

The former European champions have stepped up a gear this year though, hiring wily trainer Rolland Courbis from Bordeaux and recruiting solid players rather than stars in their bid to make it back to the top.
Auxerre will once again be a force to watch especially if Stephane Guivarch, last year's top marksman in the first division, finally settles in after an up-and-down two years at the club.
Despite losing Courbis and young prodigy Ibrahim Ba, who signed for AC Milan, Bordeaux harbour big ambitions this season, having signed no less than 14 new players.
Strasbourg, the first soccer team run by giant sports promoter IMG-McCormack, are expected to be one of the leading outsiders.

The number of teams in the first division this season has been reduced from 20 to 18 to comply with UEFA rules. Newly promoted Toulouse and Chateauroux will above all hope to hang on to top-flight status.
